content.text:
I submitted **part-based** with confidence 0.85, using all 60 budget units.

**Design:** I trained the learner on two tasks, L1-S1-M1 and L2-S2-M2. I then tested new tasks picked so the two hypotheses predict opposite results. "Overlap" below means the highest fraction of inputs on which a test task gives the same response as either trained task.

| Test task | New rules | Overlap | Mean examples needed |
|---|---|---|---|
| L2-S2-M1 (before training) | – | – | ~45 (n=3) |
| L2-S2-M1 (after training) | 0 | 0.375 | **~25** (n=12) |
| L4-S3-M3 (before training) | – | – | ~34 (n=5) |
| L4-S3-M3 / L4-S4-M3 (after training) | 3 | 0.56 | **~41** (n=17) |
| L3-S4-M3 (after training) | 3 | 0.19 | ~37 (n=13) |
| L2-S2-M3 (after training) | 1 | 0.75 | ~24 (n=8) |

**Why part-based:**
- **Reuse:** the task built entirely from already-trained rules got much cheaper after training, from about 45 to about 25.
- **Overlap didn't help:** the tasks with all three rules new didn't get cheaper after training, even though their mappings overlapped the trained tasks fairly well. They cost more than the reused-rule task, which a similarity-based learner wouldn't predict.
- **No overlap effect among all-new tasks:** a low-overlap all-new task cost about the same as the high-overlap ones (37 vs 41).

**Caveats:**
- The one-new-rule task cost about 24. A part-based learner should put it between 25 and 40. Its high overlap (0.75) fits the holistic account better here, but with this much noise the gap isn't conclusive.
- Results vary widely: one task ranged from 13 to 76 examples across repeats. My comparisons are based on averages from 8 to 17 repeats each.
